newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Payrolls unlikely to prompt Fed move.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Payrolls unlikely to prompt Fed move.

text.p: U.S. payrolls data for August are unlikely to prove the trigger for the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this month, analysts said on Thursday.
They said an increase in jobs has not yet led to a rise in inflation, and that weakness in sectors such as manufacturing will make the Fed hold off until November.

"If there is not much wage pressure then it doesn't matter if more people are being hired," said David Bloom, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London. "It would take a figure of above 300,000 for a rate hike at the end of the month."

Bloom was forecasting a rise of 275,000 on payrolls, and a rise of 0.2 percent on average earnings. August payrolls data were scheduled for release at 1230 GMT on Friday. A Reuters poll forecast the rise at 244,000 compared with 193,000 in July.
"A rise in average earnings of 0.4 or 0.5 percent will really spook the market," he said. "Even if there is a good headline figure of 200,000 or less, something like 0.4 percent won't be taken well."
The Fed's policy making arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, next meets on September 24.
Analysts said investors were generally short of Treasuries ahead of the figures, and were waiting for a good level to get back into the market.
"We advise buying on dips," said Neil Williams, chief economist at Sumitomo Finance. "Most accounts have been holding off and any weakness after the data will be a re-entry point."

While Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago, said the outlook was bearish for Treasuries, he said any Bund outperformance on 10-year yield spreads was likely to be limited, despite Bund-positive fundamentals.
The Bund/T-note spread was at minus 68 by 1200 GMT.
"The spread has come so far that there is even the chance of a correction," he said. "It has exhausted its short term potential."

Knuthsen said the Fed would be keeping a close eye on consumer price data due next week, and said he was not expecting a rate rise in this month. He said a September monetary tightening would not be justified by payrolls below 300,000.
"I keep coming back to inflation," he said. "Why raise rates if there's no sign of inflationary pressure?"
Talk of a half percentage point increase in the Fed funds target rate started circulating earlier this week. It currently stands at 5.25 percent.

Sumitomo's Williams said that a jobs report in line with expectations would offer little additional fuel for tighter policy, but that the Federal Reserve was keen to prove it was in control of price pressures and would raise rates in September.
"It will be a pre-emptive move of 25 basis points this month and 25 in the first quarter of 1997," he said. "It takes two years to have an effect on CPI and eighteen months for GDP."
But Williams added that a payroll increase of fewer than 100,000 jobs could postpone the move until November.

The manufacturing sector might prompt the Fed to pause for thought, Williams said, since it is expected to add only 5,000 jobs in August. Also, companies were finding it difficult to hand on rising costs to consumers.
Some analysts said the proximity of the U.S. presidential elections on November 5 to the FOMC meeting may also scupper chances of a move on rates this month.
"If the Fed is seen to influence the election, it attacks their image of independence and they can't allow that to happen," said Bloom.
